candidates.title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics
candidates.content: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). candidates.title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
candidates.content: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. candidates.title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
candidates.content: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. candidates.content: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. candidates.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
candidates.content: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . candidates.title: Introducing the Sakana AI Applied Research Lab
candidates.content: （＊日本語は英文の後に） Today we are announcing the Sakana AI Applied Research Lab, a research group within Sakana AI that applies the company’s research to large, complex real-world systems, advancing the state of the art in their understanding and delivering it as value to Sakana AI clients. The Lab’s first program is in finance and economics. We expect other programs to emerge in the future. A complex system, such as a market or an economy, is not something one LLM-powered agentic AI can resolve. A complex phenomenon must be modeled as a system: its units, their links, and how changes in one part affect the others. Deciding which questions to ask, what to model, and how to judge the answers has been the work of human experts, and progress has run at the speed of human effort. Agentic AI can now implement, test, and refine models at scale; its weakness is knowing which questions matter. Combining the two, the potential of AI on top of a foundation of human knowledge, will be the focus of the Lab. candidates.content: [PHASE3] RECRUITING | 申办方/赞助方: Pfizer | 适应症: Pneumococcal Disease. The purpose of this study is to learn about the safety of a new pneumococcal vaccine and how the new pneumococcal vaccine helps to fight against germs that can cause pneumonia (lung infections), meningitis (brain infections), and otitis media (ear infections) in infants when compared to the pneumococcal vaccine that is currently in use, 20vPnC (Prevnar 20®). This study will test if the new pneumococcal vaccine is as safe as the one that is currently in use. This new vaccine can possibly provide additional protection against germs that cause pneumococcal disease that are not included in the vaccines that are currently given to infants. Pneumococcal disease includes a variety of infections caused by a specific germ, Streptococcus pneumoniae. There are two groups in this study. All participants will be assigned to one of the two groups. This study is seeking participants who are: \- infants who are about 2 months of age About 2400 infants will be assigned by chance to one of the two groups to receive either PG4 (new vaccine) or 20vPnC (currently in use) into the left thigh muscle at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months of age.

candidates.title: Endogenous variability in transcription factor concentrations shapes their genome-wide occupancy
candidates.content: Abstract The control of transcription factor (TF) concentrations is crucial for the precise regulation of gene expression and cell fate decisions during development. Yet, TF concentrations can display substantial temporal fluctuations and intercellular variations. How TF levels quantitatively shape genome-wide occupancy patterns remains largely unexplored. Here, we systematically investigate how physiological fluctuations in the concentrations of the pluripotency TFs OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG impact their genomic binding profiles in mouse embryonic stem cells. We uncover distinct concentration-dependent binding behaviors for each TF. NANOG occupancy increased monotonously with its concentration, even though a common set of regions made accessible by OCT4 and SOX2 are highly and uniformly bound at all NANOG concentrations. In contrast, SOX2 occupancy does not increase with its concentrations, while OCT4 displayed an intermediate behavior. Our results challenge the notion that TF binding follows simple mass-action dynamics and reveal a core set of pluripotency regions that are bound by all three TFs at all TF concentrations, revealing how pluripotency can be maintained despite marked flu

candidates.title: AAV-mediated XIST deletion in female human hepatocytes with skewed X-inactivation induces limited reactivation of the X-linked OTC gene in vivo
candidates.content: Abstract Reactivation of silenced wild-type alleles on the inactive X chromosome (Xi) offers a promising therapeutic avenue for X-linked disorders affecting females. The long non-coding RNA XIST is central to Xi silencing, yet its complete loss risks chromosome-wide dosage imbalance. To explore reactivation in a translational context, we employed chimeric mouse–human FRG livers repopulated with primary hepatocytes from a female patient with ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency exhibiting highly skewed X-inactivation. Adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated CRISPR–Cas9 delivery was used to disrupt XIST in vivo to assess effects on chromatin landscape and OTC expression. Despite differential XIST promoter methylation, the Xi remained accessible to CRISPR–Cas9, with editing frequencies comparable to those of the active X chromosome. XIST deletion induced limited reactivation of the wild-type OTC allele and was accompanied by broader epigenetic effects. CUT&RUN profiling distinguished effects of vector delivery and XIST deletion, including global H3K4me3 reduction after AAV transduction, X chromosome-restricted H3K27me3 reduction after XIST deletion, and broader H3K27ac reduction

candidates.title: Disease-responsive promoters enable precisely controlled gene therapy
candidates.content: Abstract Adeno associated virus (AAV)-mediated gene therapy holds great promise for curing various diseases, but uncontrolled expression of transgenes in both healthy and diseased cells driven by constitutively active general promoters is a potential safety risk. Controlled gene therapy can be achieved using a disease-responsive promoter (DRP) that drives expression of a therapeutic gene only in diseased cells and shuts off once the cells become healthy again. We used correlative analysis of ATAC-seq and ncRNA-seq of healthy and diseased retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) to identify and characterize two DRPs that possess unique DRP activities in two mouse models of optic neuropathy. We further optimized one DRP to generate DRP-3L2, which has minimum promoter activity in naïve healthy RGCs, but drives potent neuroprotective gene expression in diseased RGCs and then abates after RGCs are protected and returning to health. Our proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that DRP-mediated precisely controlled gene therapy provides a new and promising neuroprotective strategy for CNS axonopathies.

candidates.title: Social predictability increases with age in dolphins: A marker of longevity?
candidates.content: by Erin R. Siracusa Social ageing research has focused on changes in average social behaviour, overlooking behavioural consistency as a trait. A new PLOS Biology study shows that wild dolphins’ grouping patterns become more predictable with age, most markedly in the longest-lived animals. Social aging research has focused on age-related changes in behavioral averages, overlooking behavioral consistency as a trait. This Primer explores a new PLOS Biology showing that grouping patterns become more predictable with age in dolphins, and links this pattern to longevity.

candidates.title: Patient-derived organoids identify PI3K-AKT signaling as a therapeutic target in sacituzumab govitecan-resistant triple-negative breast cancer
candidates.content: Liu et al. show that patient-derived organoids capture response to sacituzumab govitecan (SG) in TNBC and identify PI3K-AKT signaling as an important contributor to SG resistance. In preclinical models, PI3K inhibition with alpelisib enhances SG activity against resistant tumors, supporting the potential of PI3K-targeted combination therapy for SG-resistant TNBC.

candidates.title: Single-sequence, structure-free allosteric residue prediction with protein language models
candidates.content: Kannan et al. show that protein language model attention contains information about allostery. This enables allosteric site prediction from a single sequence and specified active-site residues, without structures or task-specific training. The approach outperforms established methods and guides experimental discovery of allosteric residues in DPP4 and ACE2.

candidates.title: BriConstrain: Geometrically Constrained Decoding for Autoregressive Brick Assembly Generation
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.33135v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models can generate LEGO$^\circledR$ assemblies from text, but their builds often contain parts that collide or attach to nothing. The usual approach of rejecting and resampling invalid placements discards decoded tokens without guaranteeing a valid build. We present BriConstrain, a constrained decoding method that restricts a pretrained language model's next-token probabilities before sampling, steering it towards valid placements. Because the validity of a brick placement depends on the non-predetermined build state, it cannot be compiled into a fixed grammar and must be checked dynamically. However, checking the validity of a brick before sampling is challenging as the space of valid placements is combinatorially large and cannot be enumerated exhaustively. Our key idea is to narrow the search space by constraining how parts attach rather than which parts attach to each other. Concretely, given the model's predictions of the currently placed part, and the previously placed parent it wants to connect to, we constrain the model's choice of how they attach. candidates.title: Depth Enables Local Entropy: Quadratic Depth Dependence in Deep Variation-Norm ReLU Regression
candidates.content: arXiv:2608.17434v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How small can a layer-sum variation budget be while deep ReLU regression keeps a statistical complexity quadratic in depth? We study Gaussian regression on the circle over compositions of $L$ vector-valued ReLU blocks of width $w$, whose second-order variation costs sum to at most $A$. With unit output bound and noise level, a budget $CLw^\varepsilon$ already forces minimax risk $\Omega(\varepsilon^2\min\{1,L^2w^2\log w/n\})$ for each fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2]$ and $L\gtrsim1/\varepsilon$. This is far below the budget of order $Lw^2$ needed when every layer carries the full gain. When $L\gtrsim\log w$, a budget $CL$ forces risk $\Omega(\min\{1,L^2w^2/(n\log w)\})$, and over a wide range of sample sizes no budget below a small multiple of $L$ reaches this risk. Conversely, every function in the class has derivative variation at most $2(A/L)^L$, independently of the width, and in a low-budget regime the minimax risk matches that of a one-dimensional second-variation ball of radius $(A/L)^L$. candidates.title: Experiment-as-Code Labs: A Declarative Stack for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
candidates.content: arXiv:2605.04375v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To unleash the full potential of AI for Science, we must untether the agents from a purely digital environment. The agent's ability to control and explore in real-world labs is essential because the physical lab remains foundational to scientific discovery. While some tasks can be performed on a computer (e.g., data analysis, running simulated experiments), Eureka moments could occur at any time while operating lab instruments (e.g., when a scientist notices unexpected clues, intuition may prompt a real-time course change). Although autonomous labs are on the rise, which expose programmable APIs to control scientific instruments via software, bridging the gap between increasingly powerful AI agents and automated lab equipment requires innovation that draws insights from computer systems. We propose a new paradigm called ``Experiment-as-Code (EaC) Labs,'' where a core concept is to encode experiments as declarative configurations that can be compiled down to device-level APIs. candidates.title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.30235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. candidates.title: CHORD: Learning Latent Spaces for Constrained Stellarator Design
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.31486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In high-dimensional, PDE-constrained design, interpolating between known feasible solutions can reveal trade-offs without repeating expensive optimization campaigns. In stellarator design for fusion energy, direct interpolation of plasma boundary parameters can violate physical constraints even when both endpoints are feasible. Learned latent representations can capture nonlinear relationships among design variables, but latent interpolation can still cross infeasible regions, and conditioning on target metrics can become inconsistent with the decoded design. We introduce CHORD, a conditional variational autoencoder that penalizes predicted constraint violations along decoded latent interpolants during training, paired with self-consistent inference that aligns conditioning with the decoded design's predicted metrics. Geometric benchmarks show the benefit of regularizing latent interpolants. In stellarator interpolation between distinct geometry families, CHORD reaches up to 81% simulator-validated mid-segment feasibility, compared with 50% for an unregularized conditional VAE and 28% for direct interpolation of boundary parameters. candidates.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.23917v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A prediction interval should contain the outcome at a stated rate. Conformal prediction sets its width from past forecast errors. When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, intervals set from errors before that break can stop covering. After Australia moved to five minute electricity settlement, a 90% interval fixed beforehand covered 51.5% of the next 400 days. One forecaster needs the next interval to cover, another a finished period's share of misses at 10%. We show that each need calls for its own restart at the date. We recompute the next interval from the $n$ errors since the break. If these errors are independent, its coverage comes within $O(n^{-1/2})$ of the stated rate, the best order attainable. For a finished period, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI). On bounded errors, if a floor under its width adds a bounded total, it brings the share of misses within $O(n^{-1})$ of target but promises nothing about the next interval. candidates.title: Scoring What Matters: Exact Feedback Reduction for Language Model Comparison
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.31931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Comparing language-model checkpoints requires estimating performance differences, yet evaluation pipelines can pay to score responses whose contributions cancel from those differences. We introduce Contrast-Aware Feedback Acquisition (CAFA), a sampler-agnostic method that identifies which scores a requested linear report needs before acquiring feedback. CAFA groups identical scoring inputs and aggregates their report coefficients, removing queries beyond ordinary caching while preserving the fully scored result. For a fixed response bank and an otherwise unrestricted scalar scorer, we characterize necessary and sufficient query sets for exact recovery of sample means, either alone or jointly with ordinary sample covariances. On controlled updates, CAFA removes 55.8% and 90.1% of the scoring inputs remaining after caching for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, respectively, averaged over four generation repetitions.
